topic: What if GTA6 physics were real?

script.text: Here's the thing. In a game, a fall is just a number on a bar. In real life, it's physics. And physics always sends the bill.
Jump off a ten-story building, and by the time you reach the ground, you're doing about fifty-four miles an hour. That's real. Gravity adds twenty-two miles an hour for every second you fall.
But the speed isn't the problem. The stopping is. A game character stops and rolls. A real body stops in a few inches, in a few thousandths of a second. That's hundreds of g.
The most a human has ever taken on purpose is about forty-six g. An Air Force doctor named John Stapp did it in 1954, strapped into a rocket sled. And he was strapped in tight.

And cars? In a game, a car stops on a dime. A real car going thirty miles an hour needs about seventy-five feet to stop. That's six car lengths. And at that speed, a car carries the same energy as if you dropped it off a three-story building.

Remember the van? It was going about three miles an hour, walking speed. To fly thirty feet through the air, you'd have to leave the ground at over twenty miles an hour. A walking-speed bump can't do that. In a game, the hit gets boosted. Real physics never adds energy that wasn't there.
So a real body couldn't do anything you did today. Which means something else is taking the hit.
Then you think about the hospital. You didn't walk there. You appeared there.
And making a whole person out of nothing takes energy. Einstein's famous equation, E equals m c squared, says your body is worth more than two days of all the energy the whole world uses.
Every time you respawn, that energy has to come from somewhere. And tonight, it isn't only the hospital that flickers. It's the whole city.

science.claim: Jumping off a ten-story building (about 30 m), you hit the ground at about 54 mph.
science.working: v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 30) = 24.3 m/s = 87 km/h = 54 mph (air resistance at this speed changes it only a little).

science.claim: Gravity adds about 22 mph to a falling body for every second it falls.
science.working: g = 9.81 m/s per second = 35.3 km/h = 21.9 mph per second.

science.claim: Stopping from 54 mph in a few inches means hundreds of g in a few thousandths of a second.
John Paul Stapp, a US Air Force doctor, took 46.2 g on the Sonic Wind rocket sled on 10 December 1954.
science.working: The sled went from 632 mph to a stop in about 1.4 s; Stapp was strapped in.
science.source: US Air Force, 'Dr. John Paul Stapp'; Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

science.claim: A car at 30 mph needs about 23 m (75 ft), six car lengths, to stop.
science.working: 9 m thinking distance + 14 m braking distance = 23 m.
science.source: UK Highway Code, rule 126, typical stopping distances

science.claim: A car at 30 mph carries the same energy as if it were dropped from about three stories.
science.working: 1/2 m v2 = m g h, so h = v2 / 2g = 13.4^2 / 19.6 = 9.2 m, about three stories.
science.source: Kinetic and potential energy, basic mechanics

science.claim: To fly 30 feet through the air, you have to leave the ground at over 20 mph; a van at walking speed (about 3 mph) can't give you that.
science.working: Best case, launched at 45 degrees on flat ground: range R = v2 / g, so v = sqrt(9.1 x 9.81) = 9.5 m/s = 21 mph. Walking speed is about 1.3 m/s = 3 mph.

science.claim: The energy in a 45 kg body is more than two days of all the energy the world uses.
science.working: E = mc2 = 45 x (3.0e8)^2 = 4.0e18 J. World primary energy 2023 = 620 EJ a year = 1.7e18 J a day, so 2.4 days.
science.source: Energy Institute, Statistical Review of World Energy 2024
